disease.name: Gallstones (Cholelithiasis)
disease.scientific_name: Cholelithiasis / Cholecystolithiasis / Choledocholithiasis / Biliary Calculus Disease
disease.icd_10_code: K80.0 (Calculus of gallbladder with acute cholecystitis); K80.1 (Calculus of gallbladder with other cholecystitis); K80.2 (Calculus of gallbladder without cholecystitis — biliary colic); K80.3 (Calculus of bile duct with cholangitis); K80.4 (Calculus of bile duct with cholecystitis); K80.5 (Calculus of bile duct without cholangitis or cholecystitis — choledocholithiasis); K81.0 (Acute cholecystitis); K81.1 (Chronic cholecystitis); K83.0 (Cholangitis); K85.1 (Biliary acute pancreatitis); K82.2 (Perforation of gallbladder); C23 (Malignant neoplasm of gallbladder)

overview.description: Gallstones (cholelithiasis) are solid crystalline deposits that form within the gallbladder — a small pear-shaped organ beneath the liver that stores and concentrates bile (a digestive fluid produced by the liver). Gallstones form when bile becomes supersaturated with cholesterol, bilirubin, or calcium salts, which then precipitate and crystallise over months to years. They range from tiny sand-like granules to stones larger than a golf ball. Gallstone disease is one of the most prevalent and economically significant digestive disorders globally — affecting approximately 10-15% of adults in Western populations and a growing proportion in India (particularly among urban women and the Gangetic belt population). The majority of gallstones are asymptomatic ('silent stones') and require no treatment. When gallstones cause symptoms, biliary colic — episodic, severe, cramping right upper quadrant pain typically triggered by fatty meals — is the most common presentation. Complications arise when stones obstruct the cystic duct (causing acute cholecystitis), the common bile duct (choledocholithiasis — causing jaundice), or the ampulla of Vater (gallstone pancreatitis), or when the gallbladder becomes infected (cholangitis — a medical emergency). Laparoscopic cholecystectomy (keyhole gallbladder removal) is the definitive treatment for symptomatic gallstone disease and remains one of the most commonly performed surgical procedures worldwide. In India, the Gangetic belt (Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal) carries the world's highest rates of gallbladder cancer — a devastating consequence of longstanding gallstone disease in conjunction with Salmonella typhi carrier state — making timely management of gallstones in this population critically important.
overview.affected_organ: Primarily the gallbladder; bile ducts (common bile duct, hepatic ducts, cystic duct); ampulla of Vater; associated organs: pancreas (biliary pancreatitis), liver (hepatic effects of biliary obstruction), duodenum
overview.prevalence: 10-15% of adults in Western populations have gallstones; 5-10% of Indians (higher in urban areas and northern Indian women); approximately 175 million people in the USA; gallstone disease accounts for over 750,000 cholecystectomies per year in the USA alone; in India: 15-20% of urban North Indian women over 40 years; Gangetic belt (UP, Bihar) has extremely high rates of both gallstones and gallbladder cancer
overview.age_group: All ages; incidence increases with age; rare before 20 years; peak prevalence in women aged 40-60 years; men affected at older ages (60-70 years); 'the rule of 5 Fs': Fat, Female, Forty, Fertile, Fair
overview.is_curable_note: Symptomatic gallstones are cured by cholecystectomy (gallbladder removal); CBD stones are treated by ERCP; asymptomatic stones may not require treatment
overview.is_chronic_note: Gallstones once formed are lifelong without treatment; biliary colic recurs in 70% within 2 years without surgery; silent stones may remain asymptomatic indefinitely
overview.key_fact: Gallbladder cancer is the most common biliary tract cancer in India and the 5th most common GI cancer — with the world's highest incidence in the Gangetic belt (Delhi, UP, Bihar, West Bengal). It arises almost exclusively on a background of gallstones and chronic cholecystitis. Early cholecystectomy for symptomatic gallstones in high-risk populations is therefore both therapeutic AND potentially life-saving as a cancer prevention strategy.

types.name: Cholesterol Gallstones
types.description: The most common type — accounting for 80-85% of gallstones in Western countries and an increasing proportion in India (particularly in urban populations adopting Western diets). Cholesterol gallstones form when bile becomes supersaturated with cholesterol relative to bile salts and phospholipids — the solubilising components. When the cholesterol saturation index exceeds the capacity of bile salts and lecithin to keep cholesterol in solution, cholesterol precipitates into monohydrate crystals, which then nucleate and grow into macroscopic stones.
types.composition: Predominantly cholesterol (>70% cholesterol by weight); may contain variable amounts of calcium carbonate, phosphate, or bilirubin
types.macroscopic_appearance: Typically large (single or few), oval or round, pale yellow to light brown; often faceted when multiple (touching surfaces flatten); may be solitary (large, 'lonely stone') or multiple; floating or sinking in water (density less than or equal to bile)
types.radiological_appearance: Radiolucent (not visible on plain X-ray); visible on ultrasound; 10-15% have calcified rim visible on X-ray (calcium carbonate coating)
formation_mechanisms: Hepatic hypersecretion of cholesterol into bile — excess cholesterol production (obesity, diabetes, rapid weight loss, oestrogen therapy)

Reduced bile salt pool — impaired bile salt synthesis; terminal ileum disease or resection (reduces bile salt reabsorption in enterohepatic circulation); long-term TPN (impairs enterohepatic circulation)

Gallbladder hypomotility (stasis) — delayed gallbladder emptying allows cholesterol supersaturation time to crystallise; impaired fasting/postprandial contractions; prolonged fasting; TPN; pregnancy; vagotomy
Mucin hypersecretion — gallbladder mucin gel acts as nucleating matrix for cholesterol crystal growth; mucin hypersecretion is an early event in gallstone formation
Shortened nucleation time — impaired anti-nucleating factors in bile (apolipoprotein A-I, A-II); enhanced pro-nucleating factors (fibronectin, IgG, glycoproteins)
types.risk_factors_specific: Obesity; female sex; oestrogen (pregnancy, OCP, HRT); diabetes mellitus; rapid weight loss (>1.5 kg/week mobilises cholesterol into bile); hyperlipidaemia; Western diet (low fibre, high saturated fat); metabolic syndrome; ileal disease or resection; total parenteral nutrition

types.name: Black Pigment Gallstones
types.description: Composed primarily of insoluble calcium bilirubinate polymer with varying amounts of calcium phosphate and calcium carbonate. Black pigment stones form when there is excess unconjugated bilirubin in bile (from haemolysis) that precipitates with calcium. They are always formed within the gallbladder and are strongly associated with chronic haemolytic conditions.
types.composition: Calcium bilirubinate polymer; calcium carbonate; calcium phosphate; small amounts of cholesterol (<20%); no cholesterol crystals
types.macroscopic_appearance: Small (2-5 mm typically), multiple, jet black, irregular or spiculated surface; often numerous (hundreds); very hard; jet black on cut surface
types.radiological_appearance: Frequently radiopaque on plain X-ray (visible in 40-50% of cases — calcium content) — important distinguishing feature from cholesterol stones; echogenic on ultrasound with posterior acoustic shadowing
associated_conditions: Chronic haemolytic anaemia — sickle cell disease (most important; up to 70% of sickle cell patients develop pigment stones by age 30); hereditary spherocytosis; thalassaemia; G6PD deficiency; malaria (especially in India — increased RBC turnover)
Cirrhosis — impaired hepatic conjugation of bilirubin; hepatic dysfunction increases unconjugated bilirubin in bile
Ileal disease or resection — increased colonic absorption of deconjugated bilirubin
types.treatment_note: Black pigment stones are NOT amenable to bile acid dissolution therapy (no cholesterol component) — surgery (laparoscopic cholecystectomy) is the only effective treatment

types.name: Brown Pigment Gallstones
types.description: Formed primarily in the bile ducts (intrahepatic and extrahepatic) rather than the gallbladder — an important distinguishing feature. Brown pigment stones are strongly associated with biliary tract infection and parasitic infestation. Bacteria (particularly E. coli and Klebsiella) produce beta-glucuronidase enzyme which deconjugates bilirubin diglucuronide back to insoluble unconjugated bilirubin — which then precipitates with calcium as calcium bilirubinate; bacterial phospholipases also degrade lecithin to palmitate and stearate which form calcium soaps. Brown stones are the most common primary ductal stones found in Southeast Asia and India — particularly associated with Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm) and Clonorchis sinensis (liver fluke) biliary infestation.
types.composition: Calcium bilirubinate; calcium palmitate and stearate (calcium soaps from fatty acid precipitation); mucin; bacterial ghosts (dead bacteria)
types.macroscopic_appearance: Soft, crumbly, earthy brown, easily crushed between fingers; variable size; often found in intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts rather than gallbladder; may be numerous
types.radiological_appearance: Usually radiolucent on plain X-ray (low calcium content compared to black stones); visible on ultrasound
associated_conditions: Biliary tract infection (E. coli, Klebsiella, Bacteroides, Clostridium)
Biliary parasitic infestation — Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm entering common bile duct via ampulla — very common cause in India); Clonorchis sinensis (Oriental liver fluke); Opisthorchis species
Biliary strictures (creates biliary stasis and infection)
Recurrent pyogenic cholangiohepatitis (RPH) — a specific syndrome in Southeast Asia and India characterised by recurrent brown stone formation, biliary strictures, and cholangitis
types.india_note: Brown pigment primary ductal stones are important in India due to high prevalence of intestinal parasitism (Ascaris migration into bile ducts) and recurrent pyogenic cholangiohepatitis; differs from Western biliary stone disease

types.name: Asymptomatic (Silent) Gallstones
types.description: The large majority (70-80%) of all people with gallstones have NO symptoms at diagnosis — the stones are found incidentally on abdominal ultrasound performed for another indication. Silent gallstones require no treatment in most cases — the annual risk of developing symptoms is approximately 1-3% per year, declining with time; cumulative 20-year risk of developing symptoms is only about 20%. However, silent gallstones are not benign in all populations — in the Gangetic belt of India (and in certain high-risk groups), the risk of gallbladder cancer complicating chronic asymptomatic gallstone disease is significantly elevated, changing the risk-benefit calculation for prophylactic cholecystectomy.
types.management_philosophy: The natural history of asymptomatic gallstones is generally benign; most international guidelines recommend conservative management (watchful waiting) for truly asymptomatic stones in otherwise healthy patients; exceptions include: gallstones in high-risk areas for gallbladder cancer; specific comorbidities; patient preference after counselling
prophylactic_cholecystectomy_indications: Gallstones in the Gangetic belt (North India, particularly UP, Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal) — high gallbladder cancer risk warrants early cholecystectomy; even single asymptomatic stones in young adults in this region may justify surgery
Large gallstones (>3 cm diameter) — significantly higher gallbladder cancer risk; some guidelines suggest prophylactic cholecystectomy
Gallbladder polyps >10 mm (or >6 mm with gallstones) — polyps with gallstones have higher cancer risk
Porcelain gallbladder (diffuse gallbladder wall calcification) — historical association with cancer, though selective calcification (patchy) has lower risk than complete calcification
Patients with sickle cell disease — prophylactic cholecystectomy often recommended at time of splenectomy or when undergoing other abdominal surgery
Patients undergoing bariatric surgery — concurrent cholecystectomy considered given very high post-bariatric gallstone risk
Immunocompromised patients (post-transplant, HIV) — higher risk of complicated cholecystitis; lower threshold for prophylactic surgery
Anomalous pancreatobiliary duct junction (APBDJ) — congenital anatomical variant with very high gallbladder cancer risk even without stones

types.name: Biliary Colic — Symptomatic Gallstones
types.description: The typical symptomatic presentation of gallstone disease — episodic pain from transient obstruction of the cystic duct by a gallstone. When a stone migrates from the gallbladder lumen into the cystic duct (the narrow tube connecting the gallbladder to the common bile duct), the gallbladder contracts vigorously against the obstruction — generating severe colicky pain. The term 'biliary colic' is a misnomer — the pain is NOT truly colicky (i.e., it does NOT come and go in waves like intestinal or ureteric colic); it is constant and sustained, lasting 30 minutes to 6 hours, then subsides when the stone either passes into the CBD or falls back into the gallbladder lumen. Recurrence is very common (70% within 2 years).
types.pain_characteristics: Right upper quadrant or epigastric; constant (not colicky despite the name); severe, cramping, 'gripping' quality; typically lasts 30 minutes to 6 hours (if >6 hours, suspect acute cholecystitis); may radiate to right shoulder tip (referred via phrenic nerve — C4 dermatome) or right subscapular region (back); typically post-prandial (30-60 minutes after fatty meal); often nocturnal (wakes patient from sleep); associated with nausea and vomiting
types.triggers: Fatty, fried, or rich foods (fat triggers CCK release → vigorous gallbladder contraction); large meals; alcohol; any sudden increase in CCK secretion
types.management: Definitive: laparoscopic cholecystectomy (standard of care for recurrent biliary colic); Symptomatic: diclofenac (NSAID — first-line for acute biliary colic pain; reduces gallbladder smooth muscle spasm via prostaglandin inhibition); hyoscine butylbromide (Buscopan — antispasmodic); opioids for severe pain

types.name: Acute Cholecystitis
types.description: Acute inflammation of the gallbladder — the most common complication of gallstone disease, occurring when persistent obstruction of the cystic duct leads to chemical inflammation (bile stasis and concentration), mucosal injury, and secondary bacterial infection. Initially chemical (non-infectious) inflammation, evolving to bacterial superinfection within hours to days. Acute cholecystitis requires hospital admission and, in the majority of patients, surgical management.
types.pathogenesis: Gallstone impacted in cystic duct → bile stasis → bile salt concentration → mucosal injury → prostaglandin-mediated inflammation → oedema and distension of gallbladder wall → secondary bacterial translocation from gut (E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterococcus, Bacteroides) → empyema (pus) or gangrene if untreated
types.clinical_features: Persistent RUQ pain (unlike biliary colic — does NOT resolve within 6 hours); fever (38-39°C); nausea and vomiting; MURPHY'S SIGN (positive in 90% of acute cholecystitis): examiner presses two fingers into RUQ while patient breathes in deeply — sharp pain and inspiratory arrest when inflamed gallbladder contacts examiner's fingers — highly specific for acute cholecystitis; RUQ guarding; elevated WBC and CRP; mild elevation of LFTs (mainly ALP)
grades_tokyo_guidelines: Grade I (Mild): Uncomplicated acute cholecystitis in healthy patient; responds to antibiotics and conservative management; early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 72 hours preferred

Grade II (Moderate): Marked local inflammation; elevated WBC >18,000; symptoms >72 hours; pericholecystic abscess; difficult laparoscopic cholecystectomy anticipated; manage with antibiotics ± percutaneous cholecystostomy; interval cholecystectomy after 6 weeks

Grade III (Severe): Organ dysfunction (respiratory, renal, hepatic, coagulation, cardiovascular, neurological failure); septic shock; requires ICU; percutaneous cholecystostomy as bridge; delayed cholecystectomy
types.acalculous_cholecystitis: Acute cholecystitis WITHOUT gallstones — accounts for 5-10% of acute cholecystitis; occurs in critically ill patients (ICU, trauma, major surgery, burns); pathogenesis: gallbladder ischaemia, bile stasis, concentrated bile in hypoperfused gallbladder; very high mortality (30-50%); diagnosed on ultrasound (thickened gallbladder wall, pericholecystic fluid, no stones); treated with percutaneous cholecystostomy (high operative risk)

types.name: Choledocholithiasis — Common Bile Duct Stones
types.description: Presence of gallstones in the common bile duct (CBD) — either having migrated from the gallbladder (secondary CBD stones — by far the most common) or formed primarily within the bile duct (primary CBD stones from biliary infection or stasis). CBD stones cause biliary obstruction — resulting in jaundice, elevated liver enzymes, and potentially life-threatening cholangitis or biliary pancreatitis. Choledocholithiasis is present in 10-15% of patients with symptomatic gallstones at the time of cholecystectomy.
types.clinical_spectrum: Asymptomatic (25% of CBD stones — may pass spontaneously); biliary colic from CBD obstruction; obstructive jaundice (cholestasis); ascending cholangitis (EMERGENCY); biliary pancreatitis
types.diagnosis: Elevated serum bilirubin (>34 mcmol/L), ALP (>3× ULN), GGT; dilated CBD on ultrasound (>6 mm in patients with gallbladder; >8 mm post-cholecystectomy); MRCP (gold standard non-invasive — 95% sensitivity for CBD stones); ERCP (diagnostic and therapeutic simultaneously); EUS (endoscopic ultrasound — highly sensitive, less invasive than ERCP)
types.management: ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction (gold standard for CBD stones); laparoscopic CBD exploration (at time of cholecystectomy); open CBD exploration (rarely needed today)

types.name: Ascending Cholangitis — Biliary Tract Infection
types.description: A life-threatening bacterial infection of the bile ducts caused by biliary obstruction (most commonly from CBD stones) with bacterial overgrowth and translocation. Cholangitis results from the combination of bile duct obstruction (creating a closed space) and bacterial contamination — bacteria ascend from the duodenum through the ampulla of Vater. Without prompt drainage of the obstructed biliary system, cholangitis rapidly progresses to biliary sepsis, septic shock, and multi-organ failure.
types.charcots_triad: The classic diagnostic triad: (1) Fever with rigors; (2) Jaundice (yellow eyes/skin); (3) Right upper quadrant pain — present in 70% of cholangitis patients; the combination is highly specific
types.reynolds_pentad: Charcot's triad PLUS: (4) Hypotension (septic shock); (5) Altered mental status (confusion, obtundation) — Reynolds' pentad indicates SEVERE (Grade III) cholangitis with septic shock; mortality >25% without immediate biliary drainage
types.causative_organisms: E. coli (most common — 70%); Klebsiella; Pseudomonas; Enterococcus; Bacteroides; Clostridium; polymicrobial
types.management: EMERGENCY: IV antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem for severe cases); IV fluids resuscitation; urgent biliary drainage by ERCP (within 24-48 hours; within 12 hours for severe cholangitis) — stone extraction and stent/nasobiliary drain placement; ICU for Grade III; percutaneous transhepatic drainage if ERCP fails or not possible
types.grading: Grade I (Mild): responds to IV antibiotics; Grade II (Moderate): does not respond to antibiotics within 24 hours; Grade III (Severe): organ dysfunction — emergency drainage within 12 hours

types.name: Gallstone Pancreatitis
types.description: Acute pancreatitis triggered by a gallstone transiently or permanently impacting at the ampulla of Vater (where the CBD and pancreatic duct join before entering the duodenum) — obstructing pancreatic duct outflow and triggering pancreatic enzyme activation within the gland. The most common cause of acute pancreatitis globally (40-50% of acute pancreatitis cases); the second most common being alcohol. Gallstone pancreatitis can range from mild self-limiting to severe necrotising pancreatitis with multi-organ failure and 30% mortality.
types.pathogenesis: Gallstone impacted at ampulla → pancreatic duct obstruction → intraductal hypertension → premature activation of trypsinogen to trypsin within pancreatic acinar cells → autodigestion of pancreatic parenchyma → local and systemic inflammatory response (SIRS → MOF in severe cases)
types.clinical_features: Severe epigastric pain radiating straight to the back ('boring' through to back); nausea and vomiting; tachycardia; tenderness and guarding in upper abdomen; elevated serum amylase (>3× ULN) or lipase (>3× ULN — more sensitive and specific); may have jaundice if stone still impacted at ampulla
types.severity_assessment: Revised Atlanta Classification: Mild (no organ failure, no local complications — 80% of cases; resolves within 1 week); Moderate severe (transient organ failure <48 hours or local complications — pancreatic/peripancreatic fluid collections); Severe (persistent organ failure >48 hours — mortality 30-40%)
types.management: IV fluid resuscitation (the most critical initial treatment — aggressive early hydration reduces mortality); nil by mouth initially; IV analgesia; ERCP within 24-72 hours if CBD stone still present (biliary obstruction + cholangitis); cholecystectomy during same admission (mild gallstone pancreatitis) or after recovery (severe) to prevent recurrence; recurrence rate 25-30% without cholecystectomy

types.name: Gallbladder Cancer (Carcinoma of the Gallbladder)
types.description: The most common biliary tract malignancy and one of the most lethal GI cancers — median survival for advanced disease is 4-6 months. Gallbladder cancer arises in the setting of chronic gallstone disease and chronic cholecystitis (gallstones present in 75-90% of cases); gallstones cause chronic mucosal irritation, inflammation, metaplasia, and carcinogenesis over 10-20 years. India has the world's highest incidence of gallbladder cancer — particularly concentrated in the Gangetic belt (Delhi NCR, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal) where it is the most common GI malignancy. The concurrent presence of Salmonella typhi carrier state (typhoid infection) with gallstones significantly amplifies carcinogenesis — typhoid carriers have a 6× higher risk of gallbladder cancer. Surgery (radical cholecystectomy with liver resection, lymph node clearance) is the only potentially curative option — possible only in approximately 25-30% of patients at diagnosis.
risk_factors_specific: Large gallstones (>3 cm) — 10× higher cancer risk vs small stones
Gallbladder polyp >10 mm (especially sessile with gallstones)
Anomalous pancreatobiliary junction (APBDJ) — congenital malunion of the CBD and pancreatic duct outside the duodenal wall → reflux of pancreatic juice into gallbladder → very high cancer risk
Salmonella typhi chronic carrier state (particularly important in India — Gangetic belt)
Female sex (3-4× more common in women)
North Indian female geography (Gangetic belt — UP, Bihar, West Bengal)
types.india_significance: The Gangetic belt of India has an age-standardised incidence rate of 27 per 100,000 women — the highest in the world (10× Western rates). The region's combination of: very high H. pylori prevalence, high typhoid carrier state, high gallstone prevalence in women, poor access to timely surgery, and possible genetic factors creates a perfect storm for gallbladder carcinogenesis. Early cholecystectomy for symptomatic gallstones in this region is a critical cancer prevention strategy.
types.early_detection: Early gallbladder cancer (T1/T2) discovered incidentally at cholecystectomy for 'benign' disease — increasingly common with careful pathological examination; management differs by depth of invasion; T1a (limited to mucosa) — simple cholecystectomy curative; T1b/T2 — requires radical re-resection (liver resection, lymphadenectomy)

severity_levels.name: Asymptomatic Gallstones (Silent Cholelithiasis)
severity_levels.description: Gallstones present on imaging without symptoms. The large majority of all diagnosed gallstones.
severity_levels.criteria: Gallstones detected incidentally on ultrasound; no biliary colic; no jaundice; no fever; normal LFTs; no complications identified
severity_levels.functional_impact: None — patient completely unaware in most cases
severity_levels.management: Watchful waiting with annual clinical review in most patients; counsel on symptoms to watch for (biliary colic, jaundice, fever — when to seek urgent care); consider prophylactic cholecystectomy for high-risk groups (Gangetic belt, large stones >3 cm, polyps, porcelain GB); low-fat diet advice
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: Development of biliary colic; jaundice; fever; elevated LFTs

severity_levels.name: Biliary Colic — Symptomatic Uncomplicated Gallstones
severity_levels.description: Episodic biliary pain from cystic duct obstruction without progression to cholecystitis.
severity_levels.criteria: Episodic RUQ or epigastric pain, 30 min to 6 hours; triggered by fatty meals; no fever; no jaundice; normal or mildly elevated LFTs; ultrasound: gallstones in gallbladder, no cholecystitis features (no wall thickening, no pericholecystic fluid, no distension)
severity_levels.functional_impact: Severely painful episodes disrupting daily life and food choices; significant anxiety about recurrence
severity_levels.management: Acute attack: diclofenac 75 mg IM or IV (FIRST LINE for acute biliary colic pain); hyoscine butylbromide 20 mg IV/IM; opioids if uncontrolled. Definitive: elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy (standard of care); counsel patient that 70% have recurrence within 2 years without surgery; UDCA if surgery refused or not fit
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: Pain persisting >6 hours; fever developing; jaundice; increasing WBC or CRP

severity_levels.name: Acute Cholecystitis / Uncomplicated CBD Stones
severity_levels.description: Acute gallbladder inflammation or CBD stones requiring hospital admission and planned intervention.
severity_levels.criteria: Acute cholecystitis: persistent RUQ pain >6 hours; fever; positive Murphy's sign; WBC >12,000; elevated CRP; ultrasound features of cholecystitis; OR choledocholithiasis with mild jaundice (bilirubin <85 mcmol/L) and dilated CBD without systemic infection
severity_levels.functional_impact: Requires hospital admission; unable to eat; pain on movement; IV medications required
severity_levels.management: Hospital admission; nil by mouth initially; IV fluids; IV antibiotics (co-amoxiclav or cefuroxime); IV analgesia (diclofenac IV, opioids); early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (within 72 hours — gold standard for Grade I-II cholecystitis); ERCP for CBD stones (within 72 hours); surgical and gastroenterology team involvement
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: High fever with rigors; jaundice developing; hypotension; altered consciousness; failure to improve within 24 hours

severity_levels.name: Severe / Life-Threatening Complications
severity_levels.description: Life-threatening biliary complications requiring emergency intervention: severe cholangitis (Grade III), gallstone pancreatitis with organ failure, gangrenous cholecystitis, gallbladder perforation, or biliary septic shock.
criteria_emergency: Ascending cholangitis with Reynolds' pentad (fever + jaundice + RUQ pain + HYPOTENSION + CONFUSION) — biliary sepsis
Severe gallstone pancreatitis with organ dysfunction (renal failure, respiratory failure, cardiovascular compromise)
Gangrenous cholecystitis (wall necrosis) — ultrasound: thick heterogeneous wall, pericholecystic fluid, gas in wall
Gallbladder perforation with generalised peritonitis — board-like abdomen, septic shock
Empyema of gallbladder — pus-filled gallbladder under pressure
Biliary septic shock — hypotension unresponsive to initial fluid resuscitation
severity_levels.management: ICU admission; urgent ERCP within 12 hours for severe cholangitis (biliary drainage is life-saving — definitive over antibiotics alone); emergency surgery for perforation/gangrenous cholecystitis; aggressive IV fluid resuscitation; IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem); vasopressors for shock; percutaneous cholecystostomy as bridge to surgery in high-risk patients
severity_levels.mortality: Severe cholangitis with septic shock: 10-30%; Severe necrotising pancreatitis: 20-40%; Gallbladder perforation with peritonitis: 20-30%

causative_mechanisms_overview.cholesterol_supersaturation: Excess hepatic cholesterol secretion combined with reduced bile salt pool — bile becomes supersaturated with cholesterol which then crystallises
causative_mechanisms_overview.bilirubin_excess: Excess unconjugated bilirubin (haemolysis) or bacterial deconjugation precipitates as calcium bilirubinate
causative_mechanisms_overview.gallbladder_stasis: Reduced gallbladder contractility allows nucleation and growth of crystals into macroscopic stones
causative_mechanisms_overview.infection: Biliary bacteria produce enzymes that deconjugate bilirubin and hydrolyse phospholipids — forming brown pigment stones in ducts

risk_factors: Female sex — women have 2-3× higher risk than men until menopause; oestrogen increases hepatic cholesterol secretion and reduces bile salt synthesis; progesterone reduces gallbladder motility
Age — risk doubles every decade; 10-15% prevalence at age 50, rising to 20-25% by age 70; ageing increases cholesterol saturation of bile
Obesity — the single most important modifiable risk factor; BMI >30 triples gallstone risk; abdominal obesity; excess cholesterol secretion into bile

Pregnancy — multiple pregnancies; oestrogen + progesterone combined impair gallbladder contractility and increase cholesterol saturation; 30% of pregnant women develop biliary sludge; 12% develop stones
Oral contraceptive pill (OCP) and hormone replacement therapy (HRT) — oestrogen increases hepatic VLDL secretion and cholesterol output into bile; risk returns to normal after stopping

Rapid weight loss — either dietary (crash dieting, VLCD <600 kcal/day) or surgical (bariatric surgery — gastric bypass, sleeve gastrectomy); mobilises large amounts of cholesterol into bile during fat catabolism; gallstone formation in 30-40% of patients within 6 months of bariatric surgery; UDCA prophylaxis recommended
Diabetes mellitus and insulin resistance — hyperinsulinaemia increases hepatic cholesterol synthesis; diabetic autonomic neuropathy impairs gallbladder motility; dyslipidaemia

Ileal disease or resection — Crohn's disease affecting terminal ileum; ileal resection for any cause; ileostomy — impairs bile salt reabsorption (ileal enterohepatic circulation); reduced bile salt pool leads to cholesterol supersaturation

Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) — prolonged TPN (>4 weeks) causes gallbladder stasis (no enteral stimulus for CCK-driven contraction); gallbladder sludge in 50% and stones in 30% of long-term TPN patients
Haemolytic anaemia — sickle cell disease; hereditary spherocytosis; thalassaemia; G6PD deficiency; malaria — excess haemolysis increases unconjugated bilirubin load → black pigment stones
Cirrhosis — impaired hepatic conjugation; altered bile composition; portal hypertension; increased pigment stone formation

Biliary tract infection and parasitism — Ascaris lumbricoides migration into bile ducts; Clonorchis sinensis (oriental liver fluke); Salmonella typhi chronic carriage — particularly relevant in India; brown pigment stone formation

Drugs — octreotide (somatostatin analogue — inhibits CCK-stimulated gallbladder contraction → stasis; used for acromegaly, carcinoid, variceal bleeding); ceftriaxone (precipitates in bile forming calcium ceftriaxone pseudolithiasis — reversible on stopping; common in children on IV ceftriaxone); fibrates (paradoxically increase biliary cholesterol secretion despite lowering serum cholesterol)
Spinal cord injury — neurogenic gallbladder dysfunction; impaired motility; very high gallstone risk
Native American ethnicity (particularly Pima Indians) — highest cholesterol gallstone prevalence in the world; genetic ABCG5/G8 transporter variants
North Indian female geography (Gangetic belt) — highest gallbladder cancer risk globally; gallstone + typhoid carrier combination

symptoms.overview: The spectrum of gallstone disease ranges from complete silence (the majority) to acute life-threatening emergencies. The key to diagnosis is recognising the characteristic pattern of biliary pain — episodic, severe, right upper quadrant or epigastric, radiating to the right shoulder, triggered by fatty or rich foods, lasting 30 minutes to 6 hours. Pain that persists beyond 6 hours, is accompanied by fever, or is associated with jaundice indicates complications requiring urgent hospital assessment.

primary_symptoms.name: Biliary Colic — Right Upper Quadrant Pain
primary_symptoms.description: The cardinal symptom of symptomatic gallstone disease. Characterised by sudden-onset, severe, constant (NOT waxing and waning) pain in the right upper quadrant (RUQ) or epigastrium (upper middle abdomen), typically beginning 30-60 minutes after a fatty or large meal. The pain is described as 'gripping', 'cramping', 'squeezing', or 'pressure-like'; it may radiate to the right shoulder tip (referred pain via the phrenic nerve — C4 dermatome from the inflamed diaphragmatic peritoneum) or the right subscapular region (back). The pain typically plateaus in severity and then subsides over 30 minutes to 6 hours — distinguishing it from cholecystitis (which persists >6 hours). Patients are restless during the episode (unlike peptic ulcer pain which is relieved by still lying). Nausea and vomiting are invariably present.
primary_symptoms.severity: Severe — often described as 'the worst pain of my life' during acute episodes
primary_symptoms.onset: 30-60 minutes after fatty or large meals; often nocturnal
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: DURATION OF PAIN IS THE CRITICAL DIFFERENTIATOR: pain resolving within 6 hours = biliary colic (uncomplicated); pain persisting beyond 6 hours = suspect acute cholecystitis

primary_symptoms.name: Jaundice (Obstructive/Cholestatic Pattern)
primary_symptoms.description: Yellow discolouration of skin and sclera (whites of eyes) from conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia — indicating bile duct obstruction from a CBD stone or extrinsic compression. Obstructive jaundice from gallstones has a characteristic pattern: yellow eyes and skin; dark tea-coloured urine (bilirubin in urine); pale/clay/putty-coloured stools (absence of bile pigment in intestine); pruritus (itching from bile salt deposition in skin — often intense and diffuse, worse at night). Elevated serum bilirubin, ALP, and GGT (cholestatic liver enzyme pattern — distinguishing from hepatocellular jaundice where transaminases AST/ALT are disproportionately elevated).
primary_symptoms.onset: Develops over hours to days as CBD obstruction develops
primary_symptoms.note: Painless progressive jaundice (no pain, no fever) is more typical of pancreatic cancer than gallstones — distinguish by imaging

primary_symptoms.name: Fever and Rigors
primary_symptoms.description: Fever occurring in the context of gallstone disease indicates bacterial infection — either acute cholecystitis (fever 38-39°C; moderate elevation; localised to RUQ) or cholangitis (fever often >39°C; associated with rigors — violent shivering; systemic sepsis; associated with jaundice — Charcot's triad). Fever with rigors is the most alarming sign — rigors indicate bacteraemia (bacteria in the bloodstream). Any patient with jaundice AND fever has ascending cholangitis until proven otherwise — a medical emergency.
primary_symptoms.onset: Hours after biliary colic onset in cholecystitis; acute in cholangitis
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: Fever + Jaundice + RUQ pain = CHARCOT'S TRIAD = cholangitis = EMERGENCY ERCP/biliary drainage within 24-48 hours

primary_symptoms.name: Nausea and Vomiting
primary_symptoms.description: Universal accompanying symptoms during biliary colic episodes and acute cholecystitis. Nausea typically begins with the onset of pain; vomiting occurs in the majority of patients during acute attacks. Vomiting does NOT relieve the pain (unlike some other causes of abdominal pain) — an important distinguishing feature. In acute cholecystitis: persistent nausea prevents adequate oral intake; contributes to dehydration requiring IV fluids.
primary_symptoms.note: Vomiting that does not relieve abdominal pain suggests biliary colic or cholecystitis rather than gastroenteritis (where vomiting often provides temporary relief)

primary_symptoms.name: Fat Intolerance and Postprandial Discomfort
primary_symptoms.description: Many patients with gallstones describe vague, non-specific postprandial discomfort, bloating, and intolerance to fatty or fried foods even outside of frank biliary colic episodes. This 'dyspeptic' symptom complex — sometimes called biliary dyspepsia — is characteristic but not exclusive to gallstones (it overlaps significantly with functional dyspepsia, IBS, and GERD). Fat intolerance specifically (symptoms invariably triggered by fatty foods) is more suggestive of biliary disease. In India, patients often describe worsening symptoms after ghee-rich food, deep-fried snacks, or rich curries.
primary_symptoms.note: Simple fat intolerance and dyspepsia are very non-specific — do not necessarily indicate gallstone disease; ultrasound is the definitive investigation

primary_symptoms.name: Right Upper Quadrant Tenderness — Murphy's Sign
primary_symptoms.description: On physical examination of acute cholecystitis: deep palpation in the right upper quadrant (at the intersection of the right subcostal margin and the mid-clavicular line — the anatomical gallbladder point) during deep inspiration causes sudden sharp pain and inspiratory arrest — MURPHY'S SIGN. Pathophysiology: the inflamed gallbladder descends with diaphragmatic descent during inspiration — contacting the examiner's fingers and causing pain. Murphy's sign is POSITIVE in approximately 90% of acute cholecystitis and is one of the most clinically useful signs in medicine for this diagnosis. An ULTRASOUND MURPHY'S SIGN (pain elicited by the ultrasound probe over the gallbladder fundus) is equally diagnostic and performed during ultrasound scanning.
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: Positive Murphy's sign + gallstones on ultrasound = acute cholecystitis with very high diagnostic accuracy; negative Murphy's sign makes acute cholecystitis unlikely

secondary_symptoms: Pruritus (intense itching) — from bile salt accumulation in skin; often severe at night; worse on palms, soles, and extremities; characteristic of chronic cholestasis from CBD stones
Dark urine (bilirubinuria) — tea or cola coloured; from conjugated bilirubin overflow into urine; often the first sign patients notice in obstructive jaundice
Pale/clay/putty-coloured stools — absence of bile pigment from intestine; acholic stools; pathognomonic of biliary obstruction
Right shoulder tip pain — referred pain from diaphragmatic irritation (C4 dermatome); patients may initially complain of right shoulder pain with no abdominal symptoms
Bloating and flatulence — from dysmotility; fat malabsorption (if chronic biliary obstruction reduces bile salt concentration in intestine); often non-specific
Loss of appetite — during acute attacks; with chronic cholestasis
Weight loss — significant weight loss from fat malabsorption in chronic biliary obstruction; also from food avoidance (eating triggers pain)
Steatorrhoea (fatty diarrhoea) — pale, floating, foul-smelling, greasy stools — from fat malabsorption when chronic biliary obstruction reduces bile salt delivery to intestine
Hypotension, altered consciousness, confusion — signs of severe cholangitis (Reynolds' pentad) — EMERGENCY
Back pain (right subscapular) — referred pain from gallbladder; sometimes misdiagnosed as musculoskeletal back pain
warning_signs_of_complications: Pain persisting beyond 6 hours without relief — probable acute cholecystitis (not simple biliary colic)
Fever developing or worsening during a pain episode — possible cholecystitis or cholangitis
Yellow eyes or skin (jaundice) — CBD stone, cholangitis, or gallbladder cancer
Rigors (violent shivering) with fever and jaundice — ASCENDING CHOLANGITIS — EMERGENCY
Confusion, low blood pressure, or extreme weakness with biliary symptoms — BILIARY SEPTIC SHOCK (Reynolds' pentad) — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES
Severe constant upper abdominal pain radiating to the back — GALLSTONE PANCREATITIS
Generalised abdominal rigidity ('board-like' abdomen) with severe pain — GALLBLADDER PERFORATION — SURGICAL EMERGENCY
Persistent unexplained weight loss with longstanding gallstones — POSSIBLE GALLBLADDER CANCER

medical_history: Pain characteristics — location (RUQ, epigastric, right shoulder); onset (sudden vs gradual); character (constant vs colicky); severity (NRS/10); radiation (right shoulder, back); duration (minutes vs hours — critical distinction); triggers (fatty food, large meals, specific foods); relieving factors (nothing relieves biliary colic; emptying of stomach does not help)
Previous similar episodes — number of prior attacks; progressively more frequent (suggests worsening disease); prior ultrasound results
Jaundice history — current or past yellowing of eyes/skin; dark urine; pale stools; pruritus
Fever and rigors — severity of fever; rigors during current episode
Associated symptoms — nausea, vomiting (character and frequency); fat intolerance; weight loss (alarm feature — cancer); change in stool or urine colour
Previous abdominal surgery — prior cholecystectomy (post-cholecystectomy syndrome; residual CBD stones; CBD stricture); prior ERCP or biliary procedures; prior appendectomy (altered pain perception)
Medication history — ceftriaxone (pseudolithiasis); octreotide (promotes stone formation); combined OCP or HRT; fibrates; statins (protective — reduce cholesterol secretion)

Medical history — haemolytic anaemia (sickle cell, thalassaemia, hereditary spherocytosis); cirrhosis; inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's — ileal disease → bile salt malabsorption); diabetes; rapid weight loss history; bariatric surgery; TPN history
Pregnancy history — number of pregnancies (multiparity increases gallstone risk); current pregnancy status (critical for imaging and management choices)
Family history — gallstones (strong familial predisposition; 25% of first-degree relatives affected); gallbladder cancer (important in North Indian families from Gangetic belt)
Dietary history — high fat diet; rapid weight loss; prolonged fasting; low fibre intake
Geographic history — area of residence (Gangetic belt — very high gallbladder cancer risk); typhoid fever history or chronic typhoid carrier suspicion (significant GB cancer risk factor in India)
Occupational exposure — rubber, textile industry (GB cancer risk factors)
physical_examination: Vital signs — temperature (fever in cholecystitis/cholangitis); heart rate (tachycardia in sepsis); blood pressure (hypotension = severe cholangitis, septic shock); oxygen saturation; respiratory rate

General appearance — jaundice assessment (scleral icterus — yellow eyes, best in natural light; skin jaundice); pallor (haemolytic anaemia causing pigment stones); nutritional status (weight loss — cancer); distress level

INSPECTION: abdominal distension (ileus from pancreatitis or perforation); visible peristalsis (obstruction); Cullen's sign (periumbilical bruising — severe pancreatitis); Grey Turner's sign (flank bruising — severe pancreatitis with retroperitoneal haemorrhage); surgical scars

PALPATION: RUQ tenderness — grade and localisation; MURPHY'S SIGN (see Symptom 1206 above — positive in cholecystitis); palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier's sign: painless palpable gallbladder — IMPORTANT: in GALLSTONES, the gallbladder is usually NOT palpable because it is scarred and contracted from chronic inflammation; a palpable, non-tender, distended gallbladder with jaundice [Courvoisier's law] suggests CANCER OF THE PANCREATIC HEAD or CHOLANGIOCARCINOMA rather than stones — chronic inflammation contracts the gallbladder preventing distension); epigastric tenderness (pancreatitis); guarding and rigidity (peritonitis = perforation); palpable epigastric mass (gallbladder cancer, pancreatic mass)
PERCUSSION: rebound tenderness (peritonitis); hepatomegaly (cholestatic liver disease)
AUSCULTATION: bowel sounds (reduced in ileus from peritonitis or pancreatitis; absent = peritonitis); succussion splash (gastric outlet obstruction from gallstone — Bouveret syndrome — rare)
Skin: jaundice; xanthelasma and xanthomata (chronic cholestasis); scratch marks (pruritus from chronic biliary obstruction); spider naevi (cirrhosis)
Lymph nodes: Virchow's node (left supraclavicular — gastric cancer, but may also suggest biliary malignancy metastasis)

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Abdominal Ultrasound — Gold Standard for Gallstones
diagnostic_tests.description: The first-line and gold standard investigation for gallstone disease. Abdominal ultrasound has >95% sensitivity and specificity for gallstones in the gallbladder. Provides information on: stone size, number, and location; gallbladder wall thickness (>3 mm = cholecystitis); pericholecystic fluid (cholecystitis); common bile duct diameter (>6 mm with gallbladder in situ; >8 mm post-cholecystectomy = CBD dilation suggesting choledocholithiasis); liver parenchyma (fatty liver, cirrhosis, hepatic metastases); pancreas (acute pancreatitis — although CT is more sensitive for pancreatitis); portal vein patency. The ULTRASOUND MURPHY'S SIGN (sonographic Murphy's) — elicited by applying the ultrasound probe over the gallbladder with the patient taking a deep breath — is highly specific for acute cholecystitis and more objective than clinical Murphy's sign.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect gallstones, sludge, and polyps; diagnose cholecystitis; assess CBD; identify complications
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Echogenic foci (stones appear bright white) with posterior acoustic shadowing = gallstones (pathognomonic); GB wall >3 mm + tenderness = cholecystitis; CBD >6 mm = suspect CBD stone; Pericholecystic fluid = cholecystitis complication
diagnostic_tests.limitations: Cannot reliably visualise CBD stones directly (30-50% sensitivity for CBD stones — MRCP or ERCP required); image quality reduced by obesity and overlying bowel gas; choledocholithiasis suggested by CBD dilation rather than direct stone visualisation
diagnostic_tests.india_note: Ultrasound is the most accessible diagnostic test for biliary disease in India; available at all levels of the healthcare system; should be the FIRST investigation for any suspected gallstone disease

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Liver Function Tests (LFTs) — Including Bilirubin, ALP, GGT, ALT, AST
diagnostic_tests.description: Essential in all patients with symptomatic gallstone disease. The CHOLESTATIC PATTERN (elevated bilirubin + elevated ALP + elevated GGT with relatively preserved ALT/AST) indicates biliary obstruction — suggesting CBD stone, cholangitis, or biliary cancer. Transient elevation of liver enzymes (including ALT/AST) during biliary colic is common and does NOT necessarily indicate choledocholithiasis. Serial LFTs after an acute attack help determine if obstruction is resolving (suggesting spontaneously passing stone) or worsening (requiring ERCP).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect biliary obstruction (cholestatic pattern); assess severity of cholestasis; differentiate from hepatocellular disease; monitor progress; screen for gallbladder cancer (CA 19-9)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Bilirubin >34 mcmol/L = jaundice threshold; ALP >3× ULN with elevated bilirubin = cholestatic obstruction; ALT >5× ULN = hepatocellular injury; GGT elevation confirms biliary pattern (not from bone); ALT spike >1000 U/L in biliary colic suggests CBD stone passage
diagnostic_tests.cholestasis_pattern: Elevated bilirubin (predominantly conjugated/direct) + markedly elevated ALP + elevated GGT + mildly elevated ALT/AST = CHOLESTATIC / OBSTRUCTIVE pattern

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Full Blood Count (FBC), CRP, and Inflammatory Markers
diagnostic_tests.description: Essential in suspected acute cholecystitis or cholangitis. Leucocytosis with neutrophilia indicates bacterial infection. Markedly elevated CRP (>100 mg/L) supports significant inflammation. Elevated procalcitonin indicates bacteraemia (cholangitis with bacteraemia). Anaemia may indicate pigment stone disease (haemolysis — check haemoglobin, reticulocyte count, blood film, LDH).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm infection and severity in cholecystitis/cholangitis; assess haematological complications; guide antibiotic decisions
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: WBC >12,000/mcL with neutrophilia = significant infection; WBC >18,000 = moderate-severe cholecystitis (Tokyo Grade II); CRP >100 mg/L = significant inflammation; Procalcitonin >0.5 ng/mL = bacteraemia

diagnostic_tests.description: MANDATORY in all patients presenting with acute upper abdominal pain and suspected gallstone disease — to screen for gallstone pancreatitis. Lipase is more sensitive and specific than amylase for acute pancreatitis. Serum lipase >3× upper limit of normal combined with appropriate clinical presentation and/or imaging = acute pancreatitis. Note: mild transient elevations of amylase (<3× ULN) may occur in biliary colic without true pancreatitis.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for gallstone pancreatitis; quantify severity of pancreatic inflammation
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Lipase >3× ULN (>225 U/L for most labs) = acute pancreatitis; Amylase >3× ULN; Lipase more sensitive and specific than amylase — preferred test
diagnostic_tests.note: The height of amylase/lipase does NOT correlate with severity of pancreatitis — a very high level can be mild pancreatitis; CT severity index (Balthazar score) predicts severity more accurately

diagnostic_tests.description: A non-invasive, non-radiation MRI technique specifically designed to visualise the biliary tree (intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts) and pancreatic duct without contrast injection. MRCP is the GOLD STANDARD non-invasive investigation for suspected choledocholithiasis (CBD stones) — with sensitivity and specificity of 93-98% for CBD stones, comparable to diagnostic ERCP. MRCP should be performed before ERCP in most cases to confirm the presence of CBD stones (avoiding unnecessary ERCP risk in patients without stones — ERCP carries 2-10% complication rate).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Non-invasively diagnose CBD stones before therapeutic ERCP; assess biliary and pancreatic anatomy; detect biliary strictures, hilar cholangiocarcinoma, primary sclerosing cholangitis; pre-surgical mapping of biliary anatomy
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Filling defects (dark foci) in bright-signal bile duct = CBD stones; duct dilation; strictures; congenital anomalies
diagnostic_tests.indication: All suspected choledocholithiasis (elevated bilirubin or ALP + dilated CBD on ultrasound) — before ERCP; pre-laparoscopic cholecystectomy when CBD stones suspected; unexplained biliary dilation; suspected cholangiocarcinoma
diagnostic_tests.advantages_over_ercp: Non-invasive; no radiation; no contrast injection; no risk of pancreatitis; sedation not required; provides anatomical roadmap
diagnostic_tests.limitation: Cannot perform therapeutic intervention (stones cannot be extracted by MRCP — only diagnostic); metal implants may preclude MRI

diagnostic_tests.description: A combined endoscopic and fluoroscopic procedure using a side-viewing duodenoscope passed to the duodenum to cannulate the ampulla of Vater, inject contrast into the biliary and pancreatic ducts under X-ray guidance, and perform therapeutic interventions. ERCP is both DIAGNOSTIC and THERAPEUTIC — it can image the bile ducts AND treat CBD stones in the same session. The most important biliary therapeutic procedure available. Indications: CBD stones requiring extraction; biliary strictures requiring dilation or stenting; acute cholangitis requiring urgent biliary drainage; sphincter of Oddi dysfunction; bile duct injury post-surgery.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose and treat CBD stones (stone extraction with sphincterotomy); biliary drainage for cholangitis (stent or nasobiliary drain); biopsy of biliary strictures; stenting for malignant biliary obstruction
ercp_therapeutic_procedures: Sphincterotomy — cutting the sphincter of Oddi (the muscular valve at the ampulla) to widen the opening for stone passage and extraction
Stone extraction — using balloon catheters or Dormia stone retrieval baskets to pull CBD stones out of the bile duct
Biliary stenting — plastic or metal stent to bypass strictures or as bridge drainage in cholangitis
Nasobiliary drain — external drainage tube from CBD through nose for temporary biliary decompression
diagnostic_tests.complications: Post-ERCP pancreatitis (3-5% — most common complication; prevented by rectal indomethacin — suppository given at time of ERCP); haemorrhage from sphincterotomy (1-2%); perforation (0.5%); cholangitis (0.5-3%); overall serious complication rate 2-10%
diagnostic_tests.when_urgent_ercp_required: Grade II-III cholangitis — within 24-48 hours (Grade III: within 12 hours); CBD stones + acute biliary pancreatitis with cholangitis or persistent obstruction — within 24-72 hours

diagnostic_tests.test_name: CT Scan Abdomen and Pelvis (with IV Contrast)
diagnostic_tests.description: CT scan is NOT the first-line investigation for gallstones (ultrasound is superior for gallbladder stones) but is essential for: (1) Diagnosing and staging acute pancreatitis severity (CT Severity Index — Balthazar score); (2) Detecting gallbladder cancer (staging — local invasion, lymph nodes, distant metastases); (3) Evaluating complications of cholecystitis (perforation, pericholecystic abscess, gangrenous changes); (4) Detecting pneumobilia (air in bile ducts — gallstone ileus); (5) Pre-operative planning for complex biliary surgery.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Stage acute pancreatitis; detect/stage gallbladder cancer; diagnose perforation and abscess; emergency planning
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Modified CT Severity Index (MCTSI) in pancreatitis: 0-2 = mild; 4-6 = moderate; 8-10 = severe; >30% pancreatic necrosis = severe necrotising pancreatitis — ICU required
diagnostic_tests.gallbladder_cancer_ct: Intraluminal mass; thickened irregular gallbladder wall; invasion of adjacent liver; regional lymphadenopathy; biliary dilation; distant metastases (liver, peritoneum)

diagnostic_tests.description: A high-frequency ultrasound probe mounted on a flexible endoscope positioned in the duodenum immediately adjacent to the CBD and pancreatic head — providing ultra-high-resolution images of the biliary tree and pancreas. EUS has sensitivity of 97% for CBD stones — even small stones (<5 mm) not visible on MRCP or transabdominal ultrasound; preferred in patients with suspected microlithiasis (very small stones) and those with contraindications to MRI (pacemaker, severe claustrophobia). EUS-guided FNA (fine needle aspiration) of pancreatic or peribiliary masses provides histological diagnosis.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect small CBD stones (microlithiasis) missed by MRCP; pre-ERCP assessment; FNA of periductal masses; assess gallbladder and biliary anatomy; detect ampullary lesions
diagnostic_tests.note: More operator-dependent than MRCP; requires sedation; less available than MRCP in India

diagnostic_tests.test_name: HIDA Scan (Hepatobiliary Iminodiacetic Acid Scintigraphy / Cholescintigraphy)
diagnostic_tests.description: A nuclear medicine scan using a Tc-99m-labelled iminodiacetic acid derivative taken up by hepatocytes and secreted into bile — imaging the biliary system dynamically. HIDA scan assesses gallbladder function (ejection fraction) and cystic duct patency. HIDA is the GOLD STANDARD for diagnosing acute acalculous cholecystitis (gallbladder disease without stones): non-filling of gallbladder on HIDA = cystic duct obstruction = acalculous cholecystitis. Also used for biliary dyskinesia (low gallbladder ejection fraction <35% = biliary dyskinesia causing RUQ pain without stones — treated with cholecystectomy).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose acute acalculous cholecystitis; assess gallbladder ejection fraction (biliary dyskinesia); assess biliary dyskinesia causing RUQ pain without stones; assess bile duct anatomy post-surgery
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Normal HIDA: gallbladder fills within 60 minutes; Non-visualisation of gallbladder at 4 hours = cystic duct obstruction (acute cholecystitis); Gallbladder ejection fraction <35% = biliary dyskinesia

diagnostic_tests.description: CA 19-9 (cancer antigen 19-9) is elevated in cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder cancer but is also non-specifically elevated in benign biliary disease (cholangitis, CBD stones, hepatitis). It should be measured when gallbladder cancer or cholangiocarcinoma is suspected — used for diagnosis support, monitoring treatment response, and surveillance. IMPORTANT: CA 19-9 is not specific — a high level requires imaging confirmation; benign biliary obstruction can raise CA 19-9 to >1,000 U/mL.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Support diagnosis of gallbladder cancer or cholangiocarcinoma; monitor treatment response; surveillance post-curative surgery; NOT a screening test (insufficient specificity)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: CA 19-9 >37 U/mL = elevated (upper limit of normal); Very elevated CA 19-9 (>200 U/mL) with imaging suggesting mass = strong suspicion of malignancy; False positive: cholangitis, biliary obstruction, pancreatitis, cirrhosis, benign biliary disease

diagnostic_tests.description: A radiological procedure performed during laparoscopic cholecystectomy — contrast is injected directly into the cystic duct stump and fluoroscopy images the biliary tree before dividing the cystic duct. IOC detects unexpected CBD stones (present in 5-10% of patients undergoing cholecystectomy), delineates biliary anatomy (preventing bile duct injury — the most feared complication of cholecystectomy), and demonstrates anatomical variants.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect CBD stones at time of cholecystectomy; prevent bile duct injury by delineating anatomy; identify biliary anomalies
diagnostic_tests.note: Not universally performed — 'selective IOC' (only when risk factors for CBD stones: elevated LFTs, dilated CBD on pre-op ultrasound, history of jaundice) vs 'routine IOC' (all cholecystectomies); varies by surgeon and institution preference

medicines.note: The definitive treatment for symptomatic gallstone disease is surgery (laparoscopic cholecystectomy). Medications play a critical role in: (1) managing acute biliary pain; (2) treating infections (cholecystitis, cholangitis); (3) non-surgical dissolution therapy for selected patients; and (4) preventing gallstone formation during rapid weight loss. Cholangitis is a medical emergency — IV antibiotics alone are INSUFFICIENT without biliary drainage. No medication cures established gallstones except UDCA for a very specific subset of small cholesterol stones.
treatment_principles: 1. Acute biliary colic: NSAIDs (diclofenac) are FIRST-LINE for acute biliary colic pain — superior to opioids in multiple trials; reduce gallbladder smooth muscle spasm; diclofenac 75 mg IM/IV is the drug of choice for acute attack

2. Acute cholecystitis: IV antibiotics + IV fluids + analgesia + early surgery (within 72 hours) is the Tokyo Guidelines recommended management; antibiotics alone without cholecystectomy have >50% recurrence rate
3. Cholangitis: IV antibiotics + urgent ERCP (biliary drainage) is MANDATORY — antibiotics alone without biliary drainage will fail in Grade II-III cholangitis; drainage is the definitive treatment
4. Gallstone pancreatitis: aggressive IV fluid resuscitation is the most critical intervention; ERCP only if CBD stone still present with cholangitis or persistent obstruction

5. UDCA (ursodeoxycholic acid): useful for medical dissolution in specific patients (small <10 mm, radiolucent cholesterol stones, functioning gallbladder); takes 6-24 months; stones recur in 50% within 5 years of stopping UDCA; not curative
6. No specific antibiotic is curative for gallstones — antibiotics treat bacterial complications (cholecystitis, cholangitis) not the stones themselves

categories.category_name: Analgesia — Acute Biliary Colic and Cholecystitis Pain Management
categories.purpose: Rapid pain relief during acute biliary colic episodes and management of pain in acute cholecystitis.

medicines.name: Diclofenac (NSAID — First-Line for Biliary Colic)
medicines.form: IM/IV injection (75 mg/3 mL); Oral tablet (25 mg, 50 mg); Suppository (100 mg)
medicines.dosage: Acute biliary colic: 75 mg IM or IV (over 30-60 min) as single dose; repeat after 4-6 hours if needed (maximum 150 mg/day); oral: 50 mg three times daily for sustained analgesia during admission
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE treatment for acute biliary colic — multiple RCTs demonstrate superiority over opioids and antispasmodics; the NSAID prostaglandin inhibition reduces gallbladder smooth muscle contraction and bile duct spasm — addressing the underlying mechanism; also demonstrated to reduce risk of progression from biliary colic to acute cholecystitis in hospitalised patients (by reducing prostaglandin-mediated inflammation)
medicines.mechanism: Non-selective COX-1/COX-2 inhibitor — inhibits prostaglandin synthesis; reduces gallbladder smooth muscle tone and contractility; anti-inflammatory; analgesic
medicines.contraindications: Renal impairment (NSAIDs reduce renal perfusion — contraindicated if eGFR <30); active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding; severe hepatic impairment; severe heart failure; allergy to NSAIDs or aspirin
medicines.note: Diclofenac IM is the most rapidly effective non-opioid for acute biliary colic; available in most Indian emergency departments; preferred over opioids to avoid opioid-related side effects

medicines.name: Hyoscine Butylbromide (Butylscopolamine) — Buscopan
medicines.form: Tablet (10 mg); IV/IM injection (20 mg/1 mL); Suppository
medicines.dosage: Acute colic: 20 mg IV/IM; may repeat after 30 minutes; maximum 100 mg/day; oral: 10-20 mg three to four times daily
medicines.use_case: Antispasmodic for smooth muscle spasm in biliary colic; adjunct to NSAIDs; particularly useful for reducing colic component of pain (visceral smooth muscle spasm); widely used in India for abdominal colic of all types
medicines.mechanism: Antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) — blocks M3 muscarinic receptors on smooth muscle of GI tract, biliary tree, and urinary tract; inhibits smooth muscle spasm; does NOT cross blood-brain barrier significantly (quaternary ammonium compound)

medicines.name: Morphine and Other Opioids
medicines.form: IV/IM injection (morphine 2-4 mg IV; pethidine 50-100 mg IM)
medicines.dosage: Morphine: 2-4 mg IV every 4-6 hours (titrate to effect); Tramadol: 50-100 mg IV/IM for moderate pain
medicines.use_case: Severe pain not adequately controlled by NSAIDs + antispasmodics; inpatient use; opioids relieve pain but DO NOT address the underlying mechanism; historical concern about opioids (particularly morphine) causing spasm of sphincter of Oddi — this effect is clinically rare and should not prevent adequate analgesia
medicines.note: The historical teaching that morphine is contraindicated in biliary colic due to sphincter of Oddi spasm is OUTDATED — morphine is safe and should not be withheld if needed for adequate pain relief; pethidine has no advantage over morphine for biliary colic and has disadvantages (norpethidine accumulation causing seizures with repeated dosing)

medicines.name: Paracetamol (Acetaminophen)
medicines.form: IV infusion (1 g/100 mL); Tablet (500 mg, 1 g)
medicines.dosage: 1 g IV infusion over 15 minutes every 6 hours; oral 500-1000 mg every 6 hours
medicines.use_case: IV paracetamol as adjunct analgesic in acute cholecystitis and biliary colic when IV access available; effective multimodal analgesia reducing opioid requirement; safe in hepatic disease at appropriate doses

medicines.name: Ketorolac (IV/IM NSAID)
medicines.dosage: 30 mg IM/IV every 6 hours; maximum 120 mg/day; maximum 5 days of parenteral use
medicines.use_case: Parenteral NSAID for acute biliary colic when diclofenac IV not available; potent analgesic comparable to low-dose opioids without opioid side effects
medicines.note: Maximum 5 days parenteral use (renal and GI toxicity with longer use); avoid in renal impairment, elderly, and peptic ulcer history

categories.purpose: Treat bacterial infection in acute cholecystitis and cholangitis. Note: antibiotics are ADJUNCTIVE to surgical or endoscopic intervention — they control systemic infection but cannot definitively treat the underlying biliary obstruction or gallstone disease.
categories.antibiotic_principles: Cover gram-negative enteric organisms (E. coli, Klebsiella — most common) and anaerobes (Bacteroides, Clostridium — particularly in severe or postoperative cases); good biliary penetration; adjust based on culture results; de-escalate when cultures available

medicines.name: Co-Amoxiclav (Amoxicillin-Clavulanate) IV — Mild Cholecystitis
medicines.form: IV injection (1.2 g: 1 g amoxicillin + 200 mg clavulanate every 8 hours)
medicines.dosage: 1.2 g IV every 8 hours; step down to oral co-amoxiclav 625 mg three times daily when tolerating orally
medicines.use_case: First-line for mild-moderate acute cholecystitis (Tokyo Grade I); covers E. coli, Klebsiella, and some anaerobes; widely available and inexpensive in India
medicines.note: Not adequate for severe cholangitis or septic shock — escalate to piperacillin-tazobactam or carbapenem

medicines.name: Cefuroxime + Metronidazole — Moderate Cholecystitis
brand_examples: Cefuroxime: Zinacef, Furoxime; Metronidazole: Flagyl, Metrogyl
medicines.form: Cefuroxime 1.5 g IV every 8 hours + Metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours
medicines.dosage: Standard combination; continue until 24-48 hours post-op or 5-7 days for cholecystitis
medicines.use_case: Standard antibiotic combination for acute cholecystitis; cefuroxime covers gram-negatives; metronidazole covers anaerobes and Bacteroides; widely used in UK practice; appropriate for India

medicines.name: Ceftriaxone + Metronidazole — Moderate Cholecystitis/Cholangitis
medicines.form: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily + Metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours
medicines.dosage: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily + Metronidazole 500 mg IV TDS
medicines.use_case: Moderate cholecystitis and mild-moderate cholangitis; ceftriaxone has excellent gram-negative coverage and convenient once-daily dosing; widely available in India; remember ceftriaxone itself can cause biliary pseudolithiasis — avoid prolonged courses if possible
medicines.note: CAUTION: Ceftriaxone precipitates in bile (calcium-ceftriaxone pseudolithiasis) — use shortest course necessary; switch to oral when appropriate

medicines.name: Piperacillin-Tazobactam (Pip-Tazo) — Severe Cholecystitis / Cholangitis
medicines.dosage: 4.5 g IV every 6 hours for severe infection; 4.5 g every 8 hours for moderate infection
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE for severe acute cholecystitis (Tokyo Grade III) and Grade II-III cholangitis; broad spectrum covering E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas aeruginosa (when risk factors present), and anaerobes; excellent biliary penetration; covers Enterococcus (important in biliary infection)
medicines.mechanism: Broad-spectrum penicillin/beta-lactamase inhibitor — piperacillin has antipseudomonal activity; tazobactam inhibits many beta-lactamases
medicines.note: Hospital-acquired infection, recent antibiotics, structural biliary disease — consider Pseudomonas coverage (ciprofloxacin or piperacillin-tazobactam)

medicines.name: Meropenem — Severe Cholangitis / Septic Shock / ESBL
medicines.use_case: Severe cholangitis with septic shock; ESBL-producing organisms (very common in India); hospital-acquired biliary infection; failure of first-line antibiotics; MDR organisms
medicines.note: Reserve for severe infection and ESBL-confirmed organisms; antibiotic stewardship — do not use routinely; send bile cultures at ERCP to guide targeted therapy

medicines.name: Ciprofloxacin + Metronidazole — Oral Step-Down / Mild Cholangitis
medicines.dosage: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily + Metronidazole 400-500 mg three times daily for 5-7 days
medicines.use_case: Oral step-down antibiotics after IV therapy in cholecystitis/cholangitis; mild cholangitis managed entirely orally; community cholecystitis in well-appearing patients
medicines.note: Ciprofloxacin resistance in E. coli is high in India (40-60%); check culture sensitivity before relying on ciprofloxacin; de-escalate to narrowest appropriate antibiotic based on culture

categories.category_name: Ursodeoxycholic Acid (UDCA) — Gallstone Dissolution and Prevention
categories.purpose: Non-surgical dissolution of small cholesterol gallstones in selected patients; prevention of gallstone formation during rapid weight loss (bariatric surgery, VLCD); treatment of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC — a separate condition).

medicines.name: Ursodeoxycholic Acid (UDCA / Ursodiol)
medicines.dosage: Gallstone dissolution: 8-10 mg/kg/day in divided doses (typically 250-500 mg twice daily with meals); Gallstone prevention after bariatric surgery: 500-600 mg/day for 6 months post-surgery; PBC: 13-15 mg/kg/day
medicines.use_case: Non-surgical treatment of symptomatic cholesterol gallstones in patients who are UNFIT FOR or REFUSE surgery: small stones (<10 mm), radiolucent (cholesterol) on X-ray, functioning gallbladder (visualised on cholecystogram), mild symptoms (not recurrent severe colic); Prevention of gallstone formation in high-risk rapid weight loss situations (bariatric surgery, VLCD <600 kcal/day); Post-ERCP stone treatment adjunct
medicines.mechanism: Hydrophilic bile acid — replaces toxic hydrophobic bile acids (chenodeoxycholic acid, deoxycholic acid) in the bile acid pool; reduces hepatic cholesterol secretion into bile; reduces cholesterol saturation of bile; reduces crystal growth and nucleation; slowly dissolves existing cholesterol stones
medicines.expected_outcomes: Complete dissolution in 30-40% of carefully selected patients (small stones, functioning gallbladder); partial response in additional 20-30%; takes 6-24 months for complete dissolution of small stones; recurrence in 50% within 5 years of stopping UDCA (stones reform unless cause addressed)
medicines.patient_selection: BEST CANDIDATES: small stones (<5 mm — dissolve fastest); radiolucent stones (no calcification); functioning gallbladder; mild infrequent symptoms; unfit for surgery; POOR CANDIDATES: large stones (>15 mm); calcified stones (pigment or mixed); non-functioning gallbladder; severe or frequent symptoms
side_effects: Diarrhoea (10% — dose-related; reduce dose or divide further)
medicines.monitoring: Repeat ultrasound at 6 and 12 months to assess stone dissolution; stop if no response at 12 months or stones enlarging
medicines.note: UDCA is NOT curative — it treats the bile supersaturation but does NOT remove the underlying risk factors; cannot dissolve pigment stones (no cholesterol component)

categories.purpose: Relieve severe pruritus (itching) from bile salt accumulation in skin during prolonged biliary obstruction from CBD stones or biliary stricture.

medicines.name: Cholestyramine (Bile Acid Sequestrant)
medicines.form: Oral powder (4 g sachets dissolved in water)
medicines.dosage: 4 g (1 sachet) twice to three times daily before meals
medicines.use_case: Cholestatic pruritus from biliary obstruction; binds bile salts in the intestine preventing their reabsorption — reducing bile salt load and deposition in skin
medicines.mechanism: Ion exchange resin — binds bile acids in the gut lumen; prevents enterohepatic recirculation of bile salts; reduces systemic bile salt concentration
side_effects: Impairs absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and many medications — separate all medications by minimum 4 hours from cholestyramine
medicines.note: Effective but poorly tolerated; rifampicin (150-300 mg/day) and naltrexone (50 mg/day) are more effective alternatives for severe cholestatic pruritus; definitive treatment is biliary drainage

medicines.name: Rifampicin (for Severe Cholestatic Pruritus)
medicines.dosage: 150-300 mg once daily (anti-pruritic dose — much lower than anti-TB dose)
medicines.use_case: Second-line for cholestatic pruritus refractory to cholestyramine; induces hepatic enzymes (CYP3A4) modifying bile salt metabolism and reducing skin deposition; effective in 60-70% of patients with chronic cholestatic pruritus
medicines.note: Monitor liver enzymes monthly (hepatotoxicity risk); multiple drug interactions (enzyme inducer); not first-line due to hepatotoxicity potential in already-cholestatic patients

categories.purpose: Prevent gallstone formation during periods of rapid weight loss (bariatric surgery, very low calorie diet).

medicines.name: UDCA for Bariatric Surgery Prophylaxis
medicines.dosage: 500-600 mg/day starting immediately after bariatric surgery (within 2 weeks); continue for 6 months
medicines.use_case: Gallstone prevention after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, sleeve gastrectomy; 30-40% of bariatric surgery patients develop gallstones within 6 months without prophylaxis; UDCA reduces risk by 70%; fat mobilisation during rapid weight loss floods bile with cholesterol
medicines.evidence: Sugerman et al. and other RCTs: UDCA 600 mg/day reduces gallstone formation from 32% to 2% over 6 months post-bariatric surgery

categories.purpose: Aggressive supportive treatment of acute pancreatitis — IV fluid resuscitation is the cornerstone.

medicines.name: Intravenous Fluids — Ringer's Lactate (Hartmann's Solution)
medicines.dosage: AGGRESSIVE early fluid resuscitation: 250-500 mL/hour IV for first 12-24 hours in moderate-severe pancreatitis; target: urine output >0.5 mL/kg/hour; reassess frequently to avoid fluid overload; total fluid requirement typically 3-6L in first 24 hours
medicines.use_case: MOST CRITICAL initial treatment for acute gallstone pancreatitis — prevents pancreatic necrosis (caused by pancreatic microvascular ischaemia); Ringer's Lactate (Hartmann's) is preferred over normal saline (reduces systemic inflammatory response and organ failure vs normal saline — WATERFALL trial: Ringer's Lactate reduces SIRS rate and organ failure)
medicines.note: Early aggressive IV fluid resuscitation within the first 12-24 hours is the single most important intervention in acute pancreatitis — more important than any specific medication; reassess fluid status every 2-4 hours and adjust

medicines.name: Analgesia for Gallstone Pancreatitis
medicines.dosage: IV diclofenac 75 mg + IV tramadol 100 mg; escalate to morphine PCA (patient-controlled analgesia) if needed; adequate pain control reduces sympathetic response and stress-induced worsening
medicines.use_case: Adequate analgesia is important in acute pancreatitis — pain control reduces sympathetic activation; IV opioids for severe pain; no evidence that any specific opioid is superior

medicines.name: Rectal Indomethacin — Post-ERCP Pancreatitis Prevention
medicines.dosage: 100 mg rectal suppository immediately after ERCP (before patient leaves the procedure room)
medicines.use_case: Prevention of post-ERCP pancreatitis — the most common complication of ERCP (3-5%); indomethacin suppository reduces post-ERCP pancreatitis risk by 50-60% via prostaglandin inhibition and reduction of pancreatic duct pressure
medicines.evidence: Elmunzer et al. RCT (NEJM 2012): rectal indomethacin 100 mg significantly reduced post-ERCP pancreatitis (9.2% → 4.4%); now STANDARD OF CARE at all ERCP procedures worldwide
medicines.note: Every patient undergoing ERCP should receive rectal indomethacin unless contraindicated (NSAID allergy, renal impairment, active peptic ulcer)

surgical_and_procedural_treatments.overview: Surgery and endoscopic procedures are the definitive treatments for gallstone disease — medications manage symptoms and complications but do not remove the stones. The choice and timing of intervention depends on the clinical scenario.

procedures.description: Keyhole removal of the gallbladder through 3-4 small (5-10 mm) abdominal incisions using a camera and laparoscopic instruments. The most commonly performed abdominal operation worldwide. Performed under general anaesthesia; day surgery or overnight admission in uncomplicated cases. The gallbladder with all its stones is removed entirely — preventing recurrence of biliary colic, cholecystitis, and gallbladder cancer.
procedures.indications: Symptomatic gallstones (biliary colic — recurrent episodes); acute cholecystitis (within 72 hours — early cholecystectomy preferred over delayed); gallstone pancreatitis (same admission for mild pancreatitis; after recovery for severe); choledocholithiasis (after ERCP stone extraction — cholecystectomy within same admission or within 2 weeks); asymptomatic stones in high-risk groups (Gangetic belt, large stones >3 cm, porcelain GB)
procedures.timing: Early (within 72 hours) for acute cholecystitis: reduces hospital stay, conversion to open, and complications vs delayed (6 weeks); same admission for mild gallstone pancreatitis
procedures.complications: Bile duct injury (most feared — 0.3-0.5%; requires biliary repair); haemorrhage; port site hernia; bile leak; bowel injury; conversion to open cholecystectomy (5% in elective cases; higher in emergency)
procedures.india_availability: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is available at all major government and private hospitals in India; waiting times at government hospitals can be long — private hospitals have shorter waits; cost approximately Rs 30,000-1,00,000 depending on facility

procedures.description: Traditional 'open' removal of the gallbladder through a right subcostal (Kocher) incision. Now rarely performed as the primary approach — replaced by laparoscopic technique. Indications for open approach: failed laparoscopic approach (conversion); severe acute cholecystitis with gangrenous changes; suspected gallbladder cancer (requires radical resection); complex bile duct injury during laparoscopy.
procedures.recovery: Longer recovery (5-7 days hospital; 4-6 weeks return to activity) vs laparoscopic (1-2 days hospital; 1-2 weeks return to activity)

procedures.procedure: ERCP with Sphincterotomy and Stone Extraction
procedures.description: Endoscopic removal of CBD stones via the duodenoscope. A sphincterotomy (cutting the sphincter of Oddi) widens the duodenal opening of the CBD; stones are then extracted using balloon catheters or Dormia baskets under fluoroscopy. Definitive treatment for choledocholithiasis and urgent management of cholangitis.
procedures.indications: CBD stones (primary indication); ascending cholangitis (urgent drainage); biliary pancreatitis with persistent obstruction; bile duct strictures (stenting)
